extracted.intended_audience: scientists, medical researchers, and historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for good experimental and theoretical work in bacteriology, immunisation, and infectious-disease research (methods, standardisation, proof of causation, and practical evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory fruitfulness and predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The characteristic of erroneous theories is the impossibility of ever foreseeing new facts; whenever such a fact is discovered, those theories have to be grafted with further hypotheses in order to account for them. True theories, on the contrary, are the expression of actual facts and are characterised by being able to predict new facts ... In a word, the characteristic of a true theory is its fruitfulness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ability to predict novel observations and to generate fruitful consequences as a primary criterion when judging theoretical claims; theories that require ad hoc hypotheses to accommodate new facts are suspect. Examples and evaluative language in the text emphasise predictive success as a hallmark of scientific truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous exclusion of contamination in experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Pasteur’s experimental method included explicitly excluding germs from flasks of organic fluids to test spontaneous generation: “I have excluded from my flasks of organic fluids ... the germs which float in the air, I have excluded from them life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to eliminate contamination (controls, sterile technique, physical barriers) when testing hypotheses about the origin or presence of microbes. Demonstrable exclusion of environmental contaminants is central to valid inference (example: Pasteur’s decisive experiments against spontaneous generation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain and use pure cultures to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Koch’s simple methods for bacterial cultivation enabling ‘pure cultures’ are cited as crucial: solidifying a medium to imprison microbes and obtain pure cultures; Pasteur and others applied Koch’s methods to revolutionise disease causation studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require isolation and cultivation of organisms in pure culture (or equivalent modern standards) as key evidence linking a microbe to a disease. Evaluate whether appropriate culture methods, isolation, and replication were performed and reported. The text presents Koch’s principle as foundational for demonstrating specificity and causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of disease causation
rubrics_metrics.description: “By degrees the fundamental doctrine of the specificity of disease became firmly established ... diseases vary from differences in cause rather than from the intensity of the cause or the environment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether investigators seek and demonstrate a specific agent–disease relationship rather than attributing variation to non-specific factors. Evidence should distinguish agents responsible for different clinical pictures (historical examples: anthrax, cholera, diphtheria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardisation and quantification of infectious agents and vaccines
rubrics_metrics.description: Pasteur standardised diseases and vaccines: by attenuating and restoring virulence in controlled sequences he could “standardise diseases in flasks: able to make and to store vaccines, exactly graduated by a fixed scale of their strength.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value procedures that quantify and standardise infectious inocula and vaccine potency (graduated scales of strength, reproducible preparations). Evaluate whether doses, attenuation levels, and storage are specified and reproducible; standardisation supports comparability and safety in prophylactic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of attenuation and documented methods to produce attenuated agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Attenuation methods are described: lowering virulence by prolonged incubation (fowl cholera), passage through other species (swine erysipelas), altering incubation temperature (anthrax), and preserving a graded series of virus strengths by drying cords (rabies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing vaccine or attenuation claims, check that the method of attenuation is explicitly described, reproducible, and that virulence was measured across passages or conditions. The historical examples provide acceptable attenuation approaches and emphasize empirical documentation of virulence changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled animal and field experiments to assess prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: “All systems of immunisation, whether in man or animal, when brought to the test of the field experiment, reveal their relative value ... It is fortunate ... that Pasteur’s activities ... were solely concerned with veterinary disease. There he had full scope for animal experiment on the large scale and he could assess at will the value of a prophylactic measure under controlled experimental conditions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require controlled (including appropriate unvaccinated controls) animal experiments and field trials to evaluate vaccine efficacy and relative value. Assessors should look for large-scale, controlled comparisons and real-world testing rather than relying solely on laboratory demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer empirical experimental proof over speculative/miasmatic explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical shift is emphasised: vague miasmatic theories gave way to experimentally established microbial causes—‘A new stream of discovery ... no longer characterised by vague philosophical speculation but by hard facts established by experiment.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise empirical, experiment-based evidence over speculative, narrative, or purely observational accounts when judging etiological claims. Look for experimental designs that directly test competing hypotheses (e.g., contagion vs. miasma) and produce reproducible results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise ubiquity of microbes and account for environmental presence in methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Pasteur’s demonstration of ‘panspermia,’ the idea that germs abound everywhere, is cited as the origin of antiseptic practice (Lister).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating studies or protocols, check whether authors acknowledge and control for the widespread presence of microbes (sterility measures, aseptic technique, contamination controls). Practical recommendations (e.g., antiseptic surgery) follow from this recognition and should inform methodological standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value practical applicability and immediate use of results
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing is more agreeable to a man who has made science his career than to increase the number of discoveries, but his cup of joy is full when the result of his observations is put to immediate practical use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess research also for translational impact and practical application—whether findings are implemented to prevent disease or improve practice (vaccines, antisepsis). Practical utility is presented as a significant virtue alongside theoretical advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, strength, and caution in reporting experimental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyndall’s praise of Pasteur’s principal paper: “clearness, strength, and caution with consummate skill for their minister were rarely more strikingly displayed than in this imperishable essay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate manuscripts for clear exposition, strong evidence, and appropriate caution/limitations in claims. Good reporting balances confident conclusions supported by data with careful acknowledgment of uncertainties and limits of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider trade-offs between killed and live attenuated vaccine approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors note: “The substitution of the killed for the attenuated live virus—certainly an expedient, but very possibly a retrograde, modification of Pasteur’s principle.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging vaccine strategies, weigh advantages and disadvantages of killed versus live attenuated vaccines; explicit rationale, comparative data, and awareness of potential regressions from original principles should be presented and critiqued.
